articles.text: First, let us be clear that the proposed Reach codes address only new constructions or large renovations. Once adopted they will set the direction for future expansions of their applicability and will be politically difficult to change direction. I show that the CO2 emission impact of installing electric heat pumps in place of natural gas heaters (whether for new structures or as replacement for existing natural gas installations) is positive. I am not addressing the capital costs and potential operational savings incurred by the homeowners. At the State of California level, the sources of electrical energy fluctuate during the day. [There is a] large drop in available renewable energy (wind and solar) at night, in the morning, and in the evening. Today there is a lack of storage facility for electricity generated by renewable energy to enable shifting that energy from the time it is produced during the day to the time it is needed that same day in homes. Potentially an electric heat pump will be fed by electricity generated by a natural gas power plant because of the unavailability of any of the other sources at the time the pump is running. However, in the first order, the amount of CO2 emitted by the plant to run the pump is the same that would be burned to generate the same heat at the home. This is because an electric heat pump furnace has a coefficient of performance (COP) of 3 in the Bay Area climate (one watt hour of electrical energy generates three watt hours of heat). and natural gas power plants have an efficiency between 30% and 38%. The proposed Reach Codes [as of August 4] may want to favor the installation of heat pump water heaters over heat pump furnaces because the hot water in the tank can be a store for renewable energy, provided that the heater is well insulated and equipped to draw electricity mainly during daytime. Such a policy has the added advantage of soaking up the excess renewable electricity that is curtailed many days during the year, as documented by the California Independent System Operator (CAISO). articles.text: We are living through the worst pandemic of the past 100 years, with no end in sight. The United States GDP shrank at a record 32.9% in the second quarter of 2020, the sharpest economic contraction in history. Unemployment was over 10% in July, and Congress has failed to agree on an additional stimulus package. Piedmont revenues are being affected. In the first seven months of this years, the dollar volume of home sales in town (per MLS) dropped $33,494,500 from $187,956,500. This represents a reduction in revenue of over $435,000; annualized, the number would be almost $750,000. Piedmont will not see the usual increase in property taxes that have padded its coffers in years past. According to the city’s financial statement of June 30, 2019, almost 75% of the City’s revenue come from “Taxes and fees”. It is clear that this line item will take a hit. Given this scenario, is the first thing to come to mind, “Let’s borrow another $20 million dollars?” It probably didn’t come to your mind, but it did to the City Council, which has put it on the ballot for the November election in order “to fund new pool facilities, restrooms, and related areas.” They approved it on August 4th, giving opponents only ten days to submit arguments against the proposition to the City Clerk.
articles.title: Not the time to take on $19.5 million of debt

articles.text: Consumer Affairs Reporter We installed solar panels in 2016 and reduced our electric bill from a really high number to an average of about $35 per month. In July 2018 we bought an electric vehicle (EV), and a few months later – when our charger was installed – we switched to PG&E’s EV1-A rate. It had low rates from 11 PM to 7AM plus weekends and holidays, but much higher rates the rest of the time. Because our panels generated excess electricity during daylight hours, we could charge our car at night and still keep our bill low. A year ago, PG&E stopped enrolling customers in our rate plan. I felt pretty lucky that we had gotten in – until we received a letter stating that we were being thrown off the plan because we had enrolled later than July 31, 2018. I thought I would choose my best rate plan. How bad could it be? The answer turned out to be VERY bad. Under our old plan, we paid about $550 per year. We had three alternative plans to choose from. They were estimated to cost us between $1,150 and $1,250 per year. So, by forcing me to switch to a new plan, they more than doubled my annual bill. How did they do this? In a nutshell, they dramatically increased the number of hours during the day when they charged low rates. Solar customers typically generate excess electricity from late morning to late afternoon. Under the old plan, this was sold back to PGE at higher prices, sometimes four times as much as the midnight to 7AM rate that was used to charge EVs. It was a classic example of “buy low, sell high”. Under any of the rate plans I was forced to use, PG&E slashed the price they paid me for excess electricity. My old bill in July was $10; the new bill was $70, a 600% increase. This makes good business sense to PG&E, at the expense of customers with an EV and solar. Solar customers without EVs have also been taking a hit. PG&E has slashed what it pays for excess power generated by all customers during the day. To beat PG&E at its own game, install a smart battery backup system. You can bank excess power during the day. There are two drawbacks. You lose about 10% of your excess power in the process of storing it and then passing it on, and it is quite expensive. The cost of a backup system can be as much as an entire solar system. Log on to your account at PG&E and use their rate tool. If you don’t use a lot of electricity, a tiered usage plan might be best. If you do, then a time of day plan may be best if you can minimize your usage during peak hours. If you have way too much disposable income, you can also install solar panels that generate more power than you use. Or you can simply move to another state. I guess we’ll have to change the old maxim to: “Nothing is sure but death, taxes…and big increases in PG&E bills.” Wiley Hoag, a Piedmont resident, is the Post’s Consumer Affairs Reporter. “The way I look at it, we have accidentally become a non-profit organization.”
articles.title: PG&E just (quietly) doubled

In July 2018 we bought an electric vehicle (EV), and a few months later – when our charger was installed – we switched to PG&E’s EV1-A rate. It had low rates from 11 PM to 7AM plus weekends and holidays, but much higher rates the rest of the time. Because our panels generated excess electricity during daylight hours, we could charge our car at night and still keep our bill low. A year ago, PG&E stopped enrolling customers in our rate plan. I felt pretty lucky that we had gotten in – until we received a letter stating that we were being thrown off the plan because we had enrolled later than July 31, 2018. I thought I would choose my best rate plan. How bad could it be? The answer turned out to be VERY bad. Under our old plan, we paid about $550 per year. We had three alternative plans to choose from. They were estimated to cost us between $1,150 and $1,250 per year. So, by forcing me to switch to a new plan, they more than doubled my annual bill. How did they do this? In a nutshell, they dramatically increased the number of hours during the day when they charged low rates. Solar customers typically generate excess electricity from late morning to late afternoon. Under the old plan, this was sold back to PGE at higher prices, sometimes four times as much as the midnight to 7AM rate that was used to charge EVs. It was a classic example of “buy low, sell high”. Under any of the rate plans I was forced to use, PG&E slashed the price they paid me for excess electricity. My old bill in July was $10; the new bill was $70, a 600% increase. This makes good business sense to PG&E, at the expense of customers with an EV and solar. Solar customers without EVs have also been taking a hit. PG&E has slashed what it pays for excess power generated by all customers during the day. To beat PG&E at its own game, install a smart battery backup system. You can bank excess power during the day. There are two drawbacks. You lose about 10% of your excess power in the process of storing it and then passing it on, and it is quite expensive. The cost of a backup system can be as much as an entire solar system. Log on to your account at PG&E and use their rate tool. If you don’t use a lot of electricity, a tiered usage plan might be best. If you do, then a time of day plan may be best if you can minimize your usage during peak hours. If you have way too much disposable income, you can also install solar panels that generate more power than you use. Or you can simply move to another state. I guess we’ll have to change the old maxim to: “Nothing is sure but death, taxes…and big increases in PG&E bills.” Wiley Hoag, a Piedmont resident, is the Post’s Consumer Affairs Reporter. articles.text: Piedmont Unified is in Distance Learning until further notice. Distance learning worsens educational inequalities. Students are estimated to lose months of learning which could harm an entire generation. What happens when Alameda County satisfies the Governor’s criteria and the school board regains autonomy? This question should be answered by all candidates for our school board. On June 24 Dr. George Rutherford attended our school board meeting as an epidemiologist familiar with Piedmont and our schools. I was thrilled because I knew he had the right expertise having published a scientific paper on reducing hospitalizations working closely with epidemiologists. Rutherford testified that with precautions, including masks and social distancing, it is next to impossible for a student to infect a teacher and that student infections rarely result in complications requiring hospitalization. The school district took Dr. Rutherford’s advice and crafted a hybrid option to allow parents to choose 50% classroom instruction or 100% distance learning. The hybrid option required daily clearances prior to student and staff participation, daily deep cleanings of classrooms, frequent air changes per hour within all classrooms, and many other precautions. The majority of parents were convinced of the safety of this modified classroom instruction. That majority persists in my recent survey as well as a Gallup survey of parents nationwide. An even larger percentage of parents were happy with having the choice of learning options. It was not a matter of either distance or hybrid learning but a choice based on risk assessments by individual households, as recommended by the Center for Disease Control. articles.text: Since my freshman year of high school, I have ended each summer with a backpacking trip with the High Adventure Crew, a coed teen Venturing Crew under the auspices of the Piedmont Scouts. Many of us had our summer plans canceled because of COVID-19, so we looked forward to the backpacking trip July 27-30 in Desolation Wilderness. It brought a larger group than past years. To prepare, we created a social bubble for two weeks prior to the trip, and wore masks whenever we encountered other people in the wilderness. Day 1 started with a celebration of crew advisor Ken Li’s 65th birthday. We met at the Glen Alpine trailhead at noon and began hiking after lunch. Birthday doughnuts were accompanied by singing Happy Birthday, and then an icebreaker discussion of what each of us hoped to gain from the trip. “I’m in my 14th year as Crew Advisor, and I’ve always loved the chance to share the joys of backpacking, camping, and hiking. Getting to know the members is a treat for me during these physically and mentally demanding trips,” said Li. With the sound of thunder in the distance, we were prepared for rain at our first destination, Gilmore Lake. Instead, it was warm and dry, just in time for a quick swim before dinner of Szechuan-inspired peanut noodles, one of Ken’s specialties. We began Day 2 with a morning climb of 1,400 feet to the summit of Mt. Tallac, which, at 7,671 feet elevation, overlooks all of the Tahoe basin. After returning to Gilmore for lunch, we made our way to Lake Aloha (3.2 miles), notable for its crystal-clear waters circled by mountains, endless rocks and trees. Surprisingly, there were no other campers in sight. Everyone decided to sleep under the stars without tents. articles.text: High school students discussing their personal stories as minorities in Piedmont in a video. Pictured are (top left to right): Harmonee Ross, August Thigpen, and Anthony Wong. Bottom left to right: Jenna Kim, Sage Mosley, and Anjuli Turner. With the school year starting, students in Piedmont will return to a classroom, albeit virtually, to study the usual subjects of English, math, and science. But some Havens students this fall will also get the opportunity to learn more about their own cultural backgrounds and explore their racial identities, all while guided by local high schoolers. Created through a partnership between the student-led Advocacy for Asian Americans (AAA) and Black Student Union (BSU) clubs at Piedmont High, and with two faculty advisors from Havens and the high school, the new mentorship program aims to provide support for students of color at Havens in their personal relationships with race. The program falls in line with the Board of Education resolution in July to create “meaningful” studies of race and an “inclusive environment” free of discrimination. “We each felt like this was something that was missing in our elementary school experience,” explained sophomore Sage Mosley, a BSU member in a video introducing the program. “Having another person that shares the same ethnic experience as you is valuable.” Jean Takazawa, an instructional aide at Havens and an advisor for the program, said she originally applied for a grant last year with the Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Committee (PADC) to create a program where Asian students could have a place to acknowledge their cultural identities. In January she invited three Asian students from Piedmont High to speak about their cultural traditions at a Havens school assembly during Lunar New Year. After that, she started to involve high schoolers in the project. The partnership with BSU was created later. A newly released video presentation about the program, which was viewed by Havens staff members during last week’s professional development meetings, features six AAA and BSU leaders and members talking about their experiences as Asian and Black students in Piedmont schools, and served as their motivation for leading the program. Ina Bendich, a restorative justice consultant with Piedmont School District, said that watching the video is “an opportunity for the community to have some insight into what [students] experience,” which she said is key to creating a shift in the status quo. PHS senior Anthony Wong, co-president of AAA, said in the video that he wants to help kids “bridge the gap between their own families’ cultures at home and the culture at school” through mentoring. Wong was also one of the speakers at the Lunar New Year assembly. Meanwhile, PHS junior and BSU member August Thigpen said she wanted to make younger Black students feel empowered, creating a more “tight-knit” Black community in Piedmont. “The culture of predominantly white schools creates a space where Black students can feel unwelcome,” Thigpen said in the video. “Not having a group for us makes us feel more distanced from the community.” Mosley, along with senior Anjuli Turner, said they sometimes felt alone at school with no one to turn to on issues regarding race. Harmonee Ross, a Millennium HS senior and BSU leader, added that she wanted to provide safe places for kids of color to “feel comfortable and valued” in ways that current high schoolers of color did not feel. Bullying was also addressed in the video, with senior and AAA co-president Jenna Kim talking about her experiences dealing with hurtful comments about how Asian kids look. Bendich, who helped start BSU this year, said she felt high school students were “a natural place” to turn to for leadership. Piedmont School District does not have many teachers of color, and high school students understand the experiences of younger kids. Wong said that the new mentorship program aligns with AAA’s goals of outreach and advocacy, and that it could grow soon to include more schools. “The larger the program, the more support we can give to our communities,” Wong said. Takazawa and Bendich both said that they wanted to include more groups of students in the future. As Havens students approach the new school year – adjusting to being at home without their peers for distance learning – this new program may help them better connect in a time when it has become difficult to connect with others. To view the video, click on https://bit.ly/3hesqmx.

articles.text: As the strangest of summers ends, a bizarre school year begins. The first day of classes for all Piedmont grades began on Monday, August 17, but without students or teachers in classrooms. The worldwide coronavirus pandemic has changed everything. All instruction will be online as Piedmont parents and young scholars face a novel challenge: to learn exclusively through a computer screen. Columnist Mike Royko of the Chicago Daily News summed up the end of summer back in 1978. “When I was a kid, the worst of all days was the last day of summer vacation. We were in the schoolyard playing softball, and the sun was going down and it was getting dark. But I didn’t want it to get dark. I didn’t want the game to end. It was too good, too much fun. I wanted it to stay light forever...But the sun always went down. And now it’s almost dark again.” The summer of 2020 was stymied by COVID-19, but still, somehow, parents figured out how to get their kids ready for the school year. Alameda County remains on the state’s watchlist, meaning Piedmont will not be able to open school campuses until receiving clearance from the county. Some Piedmont parents have gotten creative this year, learning to instill a sense of normalcy and excitement for the first day and all the days that follow, In addition to being the mother of 5th, 9th and 10th graders, Christine Schooley began teaching in Oakland public schools last week. She employs unique strategies this fall, “My three are going to head out the door and walk or bike to school each morning so when they return to the house they are ready to sit down and start school. We also had a bunch of end-of-summer ‘lasts’: last ice cream for lunch, last backyard movie night, last marathon video game session.” Some parents like Jenna Caldwell are keeping with school traditions. “We went through all of our normal motions – annual back-toschool photo shoot in front of the house, back-to-school shopping for supplies, a few new clothes, and new tennis shoes. We have to look good for screen time! “The house was definitely buzzing with back-to-school energy!” she said. Other parents have held out on some of the traditions, but have focused on transforming their new work environment. “It seems like a good year to use up some of those partially used notebooks and still goodenough colored pencils,” commented mom Buffy Yeh. “ We Lily Caldwell, who enters her freshman year at Piedmont High School, in a traditional first dayof-school photo. did get a few things to make the living room into more of a school room, like office chairs and desk organizers. The most exciting thing will be breakfast before 8:00, made by mom,” she said, smiling. Students got a taste of online learning during the spring. With pass/no pass grading and without mandatory attendance or a set class schedule, many were left underwhelmed. pages.text: Wednesday, August 19, 2020 7 SchOOLs High school students create restorative justice efforts at Havens High school students discussing their personal stories as minorities in Piedmont in a video. Pictured are (top left to right): Harmonee Ross, August Thigpen, and Anthony Wong. Bottom left to right: Jenna Kim, Sage Mosley, and Anjuli Turner. By Anthony Wong With the school year starting, students in Piedmont will return to a classroom, albeit virtually, to study the usual subjects of English, math, and science. But some Havens students this fall will also get the opportunity to learn more about their own cultural backgrounds and explore their racial identities, all while guided by local high schoolers. Created through a partnership between the student-led Advocacy for Asian Americans (AAA) and Black Student Union (BSU) clubs at Piedmont High, and with two faculty advisors from Havens and the high school, the new mentorship program aims to provide support for students of color at Havens in their personal relationships with race. The program falls in line with the Board of Education resolution in July to create “meaningful” studies of race and an “inclusive environment” free of discrimination. “We each felt like this was something that was missing in our elementary school experience,” explained sophomore Sage Mosley, a BSU member in a video introducing the program. “Having another person that shares the same ethnic experience as you is valuable.” Jean Takazawa, an instructional aide at Havens and an advisor for the program, said she originally applied for a grant last year with the Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Committee (PADC) to create a program where Asian students could have a place to acknowledge their cultural identities. In January she invited three Asian students from Piedmont High to speak about their cultural traditions at a Havens school assembly during Lunar New Year. After that, she started to involve high schoolers in the project. The partnership with BSU was created later. A newly released video presentation about the program, which was viewed by Havens staff members during last week’s professional development meetings, features six AAA and BSU leaders and members talking about their experiences as Asian and Black students in Piedmont schools, and served as their motivation for leading the program. Ina Bendich, a restorative justice consultant with Piedmont School District, said that watching the video is “an opportunity for the community to have some insight into what [students] experience,” which she said is key to creating a shift in the status quo. PHS senior Anthony Wong, co-president of AAA, said in the video that he wants to help kids “bridge the gap between their own families’ cultures at home and the culture at school” through mentoring. Wong was also one of the speakers at the Lunar New Year assembly. Meanwhile, PHS junior and BSU member August Thigpen said she wanted to make younger Black students feel empowered, creating a more “tight-knit” Black community in Piedmont. “The culture of predominantly white schools creates a space where Black students can feel unwelcome,” Thigpen said in the video. “Not having a group for us makes us feel more distanced from the community.” Mosley, along with senior Anjuli Turner, said they sometimes felt alone at school with no one to turn to on issues regarding race. Harmonee Ross, a Millennium HS senior and BSU leader, added that she wanted to provide safe places for kids of color to “feel comfortable and valued” in ways that current high schoolers of color did not feel. Bullying was also addressed in the video, with senior and AAA co-president Jenna Kim talking about her experiences dealing with hurtful comments about how Asian kids look. Bendich, who helped start BSU this year, said she felt high school students were “a natural place” to turn to for leadership. Piedmont School District does not have many teachers of color, and high school students understand the experiences of younger kids. Wong said that the new mentorship program aligns with AAA’s goals of outreach and advocacy, and that it could grow soon to include more schools. “The larger the program, the more support we can give to our communities,” Wong said. Takazawa and Bendich both said that they wanted to include more groups of students in the future. As Havens students approach the new school year – adjusting to being at home without their peers for distance learning – this new program may help them better connect in a time when it has become difficult to connect with others. To view the video, click on https://bit.ly/3hesqmx. Piedmont students return to school – virtually By Jay Russell As the strangest of summers ends, a bizarre school year begins. The first day of classes for all Piedmont grades began on Monday, August 17, but without students or teachers in classrooms. The worldwide coronavirus pandemic has changed everything. All instruction will be online as Piedmont parents and young scholars face a novel challenge: to learn exclusively through a computer screen. Columnist Mike Royko of the Chicago Daily News summed up the end of summer back in 1978. “When I was a kid, the worst of all days was the last day of summer vacation. We were in the schoolyard playing softball, and the sun was going down and it was getting dark. But I didn’t want it to get dark. I didn’t want the game to end. It was too good, too much fun. I wanted it to stay light forever...But the sun always went down. And now it’s almost dark again.” The summer of 2020 was stymied by COVID-19, but still, somehow, parents figured out how to get their kids ready for the school year. Alameda County remains on the state’s watchlist, meaning Piedmont will not be able to open school campuses until receiving clearance from the county. Some Piedmont parents have gotten creative this year, learning to instill a sense of normalcy and excitement for the first day and all the days that follow, In addition to being the mother of 5th, 9th and 10th graders, Christine Schooley began teaching in Oakland public schools last week. She employs unique strategies this fall, “My three are going to head out the door and walk or bike to school each morning so when they return to the house they are ready to sit down and start school. We also had a bunch of end-of-summer ‘lasts’: last ice cream for lunch, last backyard movie night, last marathon video game session.” Some parents like Jenna Caldwell are keeping with school traditions. “We went through all of our normal motions – annual back-toschool photo shoot in front of the house, back-to-school shopping for supplies, a few new clothes, and new tennis shoes. We have to look good for screen time! “The house was definitely buzzing with back-to-school energy!” she said. Other parents have held out on some of the traditions, but have focused on transforming their new work environment. “It seems like a good year to use up some of those partially used notebooks and still goodenough colored pencils,” commented mom Buffy Yeh. “ We Lily Caldwell, who enters her freshman year at Piedmont High School, in a traditional first dayof-school photo. did get a few things to make the living room into more of a school room, like office chairs and desk organizers. The most exciting thing will be breakfast before 8:00, made by mom,” she said, smiling. Students got a taste of online learning during the spring. With pass/no pass grading and without mandatory attendance or a set class schedule, many were left underwhelmed. Now there are set times for class, attendance is taken and new etiquette for video conferencing is in place. A few Piedmont students shared their first-day-of-school experience with the Post. articles.text: Welcome back to school. We are staying in distance learning for God knows how long. Although this is better than nothing, we all had hoped the school district would figure out a way for us to go back to school in person. Schedules were released last week for the online classes. So for most of the day everybody was frantically calling and texting friends to see if they had classes together. We told each other that it was going to be alright because it wasn’t as if we were going to be in a real building with live teaching. With no in-person learning, being trapped inside of a house with your family and glued to the screen on Zoom calls for six hours a day this school year, it is definitely going to be interesting. In other news the first of the high school buildings is almost done. I am actually really happy about that because it is such a beautiful building. But the big question many people are asking is what is going to happen with it? With new buildings that will be empty until students and teachers return to classrooms, I think that we should start a roller blade club. Bored kids can grab a pair of skates and just go crazy racing up and down in the empty hallways. Otherwise we are left with a $30 million classroom building empty and silent as a ghost. Some people think that construction should stop. I understand why people who live close to the school and can hear all the banging and clanging on a new building that’s not going to reopen for a year are complaining. Some now are asking why the bond money for construction should instead be spent for boosting our distance learning platform, or on safety measures that would allow us to attend school in person. I guess it is better to look at a new building and one just being built, than to look at a pile of rubble if construction were to stop. Now that we are back to virtual school, I wish the best to all the teachers for working through the hardships of COVID, and to the students who have figured out how to study remotely. This year is going to be a roller coaster, with ups and downs. For sure, it will be an adventure. Crystal Vacker is a Piedmont student with a keen eye and the ability to be in several places at one time.

articles.text: By: Kaelin Campbell Piedmont for Oakland Public Schools (POPS) is a group of Piedmont High School students and alums working to bring the Piedmont community together to support Oakland-based organizations that fight for educational equity. The first POPS campaign raised over $62,000 for three organizations, State of Black Education Oakland, Planting Justice, and Black Organizing Project. With plans to continue the momentum, a second campaign has been launched to centralize donations to two organizations working to combat digital inequity in Oakland: The A to Z fund, and Oakland REACH. The systemic educational divides that POPS targeted in the first campaign will be exacerbated by the coronavirus pandemic as public schools are solely online this fall. In a survey conducted in 2019, 45% of Oakland students don’t have access to home internet. The lack of access will result in even higher teacher turnover rates, will detract from parents’ abilities to work outside the home, and create more socioemotional stress on everyone. articles.text: When I think about the next years of my life, senior spring, college applications and internships come to mind. The only housing I am worried about is whether it will be on or off campus in my freshman year in college. But for 1,700, kids ages 14-24, l who are homeless in Alameda County, their concerns are focused on finding housing, education, food, and safety. The Bay Area has the third highest homeless population in the United States, behind New York City and Los Angeles. But one group doing something about remedying this crisis is Youth Spirit Artworks. YSA has plans to make a Tiny House Village that will serve as transitional housing for two years for teens age 18-24. During these two years, residents will participate in job training, community upkeep, and cooking regularly. Last year, Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC) funded and volunteered to make a Tiny house to contribute to the Village. Through this project, PCSC members learned how to build the framing for a house, install insulation, drywall, skylights, doors and windows. Participating in this project, in addition to helping combat the housing crisis, is helping the Piedmont volunteers appreciate all of the work that goes into building a house. As a Council member I have leveraged my deep community connections to engage and promote diverse perspectives, develop mutually beneficial solutions, and increase equity and inclusiveness. When my dad retired from the Army, we moved to Oakland for a short time before settling in Piedmont in 1969. articles.text: Piedmont City Council approved an agreement with Vintage Contractors for refurbishment of the Park Tennis Courts in the amount of $97,000. The unanimous approval was made at an August 17 meeting. The city’s four tennis court facilities are resurfaced, and repairs are completed on a rotation. The scheduled repair of courts began with Linda Beach, Hampton Park, Recreation Courts (now the Corey Reich Tennis Center), and now the courts in the Main Park. Repairs to the Linda Beach courts was completed in 2016. Hampton Park required more substantial repair and was completed in 2017 as part of the comprehensive Hampton Park Improvement Plan. The Rec Tennis Courts project was completed in 2019 with strong financial support from the community, led by the non-profit Piedmont Recreation Facilities Organization. The Park Courts are the last to be refurbished. Vice Mayor Teddy Gray King said it is the right time to move forward in fixing the courts. “Hats off to Sara [Lillevand] for placing this item on the agenda. Everyone loves those courts and [the refurbishment] is the right thing to do with city resources,” King said. The scope of the project will include resurfacing two tennis courts with a slip sheet overlay system, similar to the Corey Reich Tennis Center, and installing new net posts and nets similar to the courts on Vista Avenue. All Piedmont tennis courts reopened on May 18 after a twomonth closure due to COVID-19 and shelter-in-place restrictions.

articles.text: The City Council received a report on the 2023–2031 Housing Element and Regional Housing Needs Allocation (RHNA) plan at its August 17 meeting as the basis for a discussion on future housing. Since 1969, California law has required that all jurisdictions within the state create a plan to meet the housing needs of everyone in the community. Each local government must update its housing element and zoning, if needed, to show how it plans to accommodate its share of the regional need. The housing element is one of the mandatory elements of the Piedmont General Plan. Consultant Barry Miller, who works with the city to develop its detailed housing report, provided a presentation at Monday night’s meeting. He described RHNA as “a unique element, the only part of the general plan that has to updated on the cycle that is set by the state legislature.” The housing element must demonstrate Piedmont’s ability to accommodate its “fair share” of the region’s housing needs. The RHNA process is not new. In two years, Piedmont will enter its sixth cycle in the process. Piedmont School District announced the closure of Witter Field as of Monday, August 3. The closure includes the main football-soccer-lacrosse field, the baseball and softball fields and their batting cages, and the field house. Though school began online classes this week on August 17, the field remains closed. The closure resulted from “persistent lack of compliance with the Alameda County Public Health Department’s Shelter in Place orders” according to Supt. Randy Booker. Despite repeated warnings, field users have continued to play group sports in violation of COVID-19 health orders. Similar complaints led the City to close the Linda Beach Playfield last week. In a press release, Booker wrote, ”The District regrets having to take this action and the inconvenience this may cause the community. articles.text: Witter Field has been closed once again. For many, this fall will be the first time without sports in town. COVID-19 continues to force communities all over the world to change how they think and alter many of their cherished traditions. In Piedmont, for the first time since world War II, there won’t be any sports this fall. No helmets cracking and pads smacking at Witter. No matchpoints at the tennis courts. No PRs being set by cross country runners. No goals being scored by Max Wagener or Ella Wright in the Piedmont Pool. No spirit week on campus. No student rooting section. No senior nights. No taco vendor. No food booths. Witter Field remains closed, meaning the school stays under county guidelines toward official activities. California is among 15 states committed to deferring all high school sports until 2021. “We still need some clarity ahead of December toward having access to kids and having a full offseason,” said football coach Jerome Johnson in anticipation of being able to start practices sometime that month. Witter shutting down has caused the budding stars of the Highlander soccer program to commute to new training locations. “We’re not practicing in Piedmont and have had to find other homes,” said Dan Chubbock, PHS women’s coach and Coaching Director of Piedmont Soccer Club. “That’s just how it is right now. We’ve had to move to Hayward and other locations.” At this time last year, the football program was beginning double days, the final preparation before its first scrimmage games that historically mark the beginning of the season. Piedmont has a five-year tradition of playing Justin Siena in the first week of the season. The Highlanders are still set to play the Braves for its opener, but not until January 2021. And question remains unanswered: will parents, students, or even journalists be allowed at games? A shining light around town is the Corey Reich Tennis Center at the corner of Vista and Bonita Avenue. The four-court complex remains open for residents and Jim Landes’ youth programs. But this fall what won’t be seen are the many players on the high school girls’ tennis team practicing and playing matches as they set their sights on another league championship. It is the first fall season without a girls’ team in action. Despite the headlines of other sports, Piedmont girls’ program’s 20-year unbeaten league championship remains among the top state records. For a girls’ team that saw that record come to an end last season, the team’s development of its younger players this year was critical. But coach Landes is skeptical about the possibility of even having a JV team because the season was both compressed and postponed to next spring. “I had over 15 incoming freshman girls reach out to me. We have a big turn out every year, and normally I’ll take 35-40 kids between JV and varsity. Now we’ll be lucky if we do half that,” said Landes. The big problem is that CIF has scheduled boys; and girls; tennis season to run concurrently, and in the spring. Piedmont has 8 courts available at three separate sites blocks from one another. If both programs run separate seasons, Landes and assistant Corey Reich would be pulling double-duty for some 70-plus kids. “We’ll have to be flexible with how we structure and run things. Running both teams is going to be difficult. If we keep teams around the same size, I would need all four courts for each practice. We’d have to do one practice followed by another, and you have to consider time availability of the tennis courts and school hours for kids,” Landes added. This isn’t the first time in recent memory the girls’ tennis team hit a roadblock. In 2018, the North Coast Section vacated its team tennis championship after the Butte County wildfire smoke and the following rain eliminated competition as schools transitioned from fall to winter semesters. This time, high school sports fans can only hope the teams reach the necessary phase to return. No tennis at the Corey Reich Tennis Center is a first for the girls’ tennis program.

Adam Low won the Posts’ 2017 Athlete of the Year award after scoring 103 goals, 25 assists and 76 steals in the 2016 season. He went on to play for Santa Clara University. With attention on a November ballot item that would raise money to build a new community pool in Piedmont, we take a look back at the recent success of the high school’s water polo program – the 2016 boys and 2017 girls. The 2016, the boys’ team under coach John Savage set the stage for four consecutive years of success and the growth of its popularity as a fall sport. In the prior years, the team went 11-11 in 2015, 8-6 in 2014, and won only two games in 2013, Savage’s first year as head coach. The 2016 team went 19-9 and reached the semifinals of the Division 2 North Coast Section playoffs as the No. 5 seeded team. They lost to No. 1 Tamalpais, 17-9. The team featured the Post’s 2017 Athlete of the Year, Adam Low, who went on to play for Santa Clara University, a Div. 1 program. That season Low scored 103 goals, 25 assists, 76 steals to depart Piedmont as its all-time leading scorer – at the time. 2016 also had two future All-American players, sophomores Henry Saunders, and Patrick Conn, who eclipsed Low as the school’s all-time leading goal scorer the following two years. One thing that still has eluded Savage and Piedmont High is: a Western Alameda County Conference trophy, with Bishop O’Dowd as the perennial nemesis. Piedmont lost in the 2016 league finals to O’Dowd 16-11 then were upset by the Dragons the following year 8-4 in the opening round. In 2018, led by seniors Conn and Saunders, Piedmont had perhaps its strongest roster of all time with a 22-6 overall record and was undefeated in league prior to the playoffs. But in the 2018 finals, PHS relinquished a 15-10 lead going into the fourth quarter to O’Dowd and once again came up short, losing 17-16. Girls’ team The girls’ 2017 team was headlined by the school’s single season scoring record, Annika Disney, who scored 99 goals in 19 games that season after missing some time due to injury. Like Low, she now plays at Santa Clara. That year the team was 10-13 and missed out on NCS playoffs. Disney had some illustrious performances, including a single-game record of 12 goals against Pinole Valley, which snapped Sarah Mooney’s record of nine goals in 2013. Annika Disney set Piedmont High’s school record in a single season for goals with 99. She also plays for Santa Clara. articles.text: Another week has passed for UEFA’s 2020 competitions, Champions and Europa league, the highest tiers of European club football. articles.text: With the current heat wave, your options to escape this tropical warmth can be few and far between with digits reaching the high 90s in Piedmont and the surrounding Oakland Hills. Escaping toward the ocean could be a safe bet, but with COVID-19, sudden beach, parking lot, and trail closures could leave explorers in unfortunate situations far from home. Going early to trails was already important with COVID to escape the heavy crowds of people in popular areas throughout Joaquin Miller, Redwood Regional, Tilden, and other frequented parks. And now add heat to the equation. Trails are most heavily used around noontime, so consider starting your trail at 7 a.m. It is already 70 degrees, but it’s better than later in the morning. Here are a group of trails and parks for you to consider to keep you shaded and out of the sun: Huckleberry Botanic Regional Preserve This 2.4 mile-loop is dug out of a canyon along Skyline Boulevard. The trail is often less than a few feet wide, so it’s increasingly important to hit this park early to avoid contact with lots of people. Make sure you bring – and wear – your mask. The trail offers just under 450 feet of elevation gain and is easy to navigate, so you can continue on a second loop for an added workout without worry. If you want an increased lower body workout, multiple long stairwells are available to create your own circuit amidst the trees. The park is an oasis for wildflowers, ferns, trees, and information on them. Along the trail are panels identifying the vegetation with a year-round display of blossoming plants throughout the 241-acre preserve. You’ll find the glistening red bark of Pallid Manzanita, fragrant groves of California Bay Laurels, Brittleleaf Manzanita, Coast huckleberry, Douglas Iris, three different fern species (western bracken, coastal wood, and western sword), Pacific madrone, and the edible California Hazelnut. Leona Canyon/Leona Heights Leona Canyon and Leona Heights are two shady conjoining parks in the Oakland hills near Merritt College. Leona Canyon has trailheads on Campus Drive and the Merritt College parking lot, offering a quick 1.7 mile walk alongside Rifle Range Creek. Hikers and dog walkers often sit next to the creek, under the shade of Oak trees and beside groves of ferns. About midway into the park, an abandoned 1940s car sits in the creek. There’s also the foundation of an old logger’s home a few hundred yards down the trail. Leona Heights is a shorter 1.5 mile trail by Horseshoe Creek, which is much more active than the creek at Leona Canyon. The trail has a graffiti-covered foundation from an old factory building and a brief glimpse of the old Leona Heights Sulphur Mine, which was active from the 1890s until 1934. Although there are no recent reported sicknesses, it’s important to mention that a portion of the old sulfur mine has runoff leading into the creek. Parents and dog owners should be wary of the water after a rain. Dimond Canyon Dimond Canyon’s Bridgeview trail is just 1.5 miles from Montclair. It spans the Montclair Golf Course driving range (considered a hidden treasure to locals) beneath Redwood trees and the usual assortment of Oaks and Bays. The trail heads down into Dimond Park of Oakland and also travels next to Sausal Creek. It’s an ideal spot to escape the sun and isn’t a difficult hike with 400 feet in elevation gain, pending where you start. For an ascent, start at the El Centro Trailhead on El Centro Avenue. For a decline that starts closer to Montclair, begin on Monterey Boulevard. Leona Canyon in Oakland will keep you out of the sun and shaded by oaks, ferns in the midst of local history. Although Huckleberry Preserve only has a 2.4 mile loop, there are many sections of stairs for individual workouts. Dimond Canyon’s Bridgeview Trail is a short 1.5 mile walk between Montclair and Dimond Park. Dimond Canyon takes you along the Montclair Golf Course driving range. There should be enough distance to protect you from bad golfers.

articles.text: Here are 8 steps to succeed with distance learning responsible for ensuring their students keep up. Listed below are eight things you can do to help your students succeed: 1. Keep a schedule Shelter-in-place education is chaotic and discordant, which can make it even harder for students to focus. To help minimize these effects it is important to keep your students on a schedule. This can add consistency and normalcy to your children’s academic lives and help them keep focused on learning. Try to maintain consistent bed and wake times, study hours, free time, exercise routines, meals, and family hours. Many students will initially resist regular schedules, but if forced to stick to it, they will often become calmer and achieve more. but cutting is cutting, regardless of the vehicle. Once a student has “broken the seal” and skips a class, cutting can become normalized or even become a habit. Unfortunately, just getting them on the computer isn’t enough, because cutting can involve anything from not logging in at all, to logging in but leaving the room, to logging in but tuning out. Since most online classes meet less often than physical classes, attending every online class is essential. In addition, since meeting with teachers is more difficult, it can take twice as much effort to catch up once a student falls behind. 5. Get a Tutor: Tutors used to be available only to those with extensive disposable income. There are still many expensive tutors available, and they can be very helpful for those who can afford them, but distance learning has changed the tutoring landscape. You are no longer limited by geography, so expand your search to the entire nation, or even internationally. You never know, a British English tutor, Bolivian Spanish tutor or Armenian math tutor might be significantly less expensive. You may also be able to find a variety of free online tutoring resources. Find out what is available through your school district, library, government, Rotary Club or other local organization. 2. Make a Classroom It doesn’t matter if it’s the kitchen table, the living room or your kid’s bedroom, but a student needs a quiet, distraction-free place that they associate with learning. Figure out where your student’s “school room” is going to be ahead of time and start making arrangements now for their “classroom” space. 3. Don’t skip class Few parents accept cutting class in physical schools, so why do parents accept it in online education? It just doesn’t seem as serious to miss a Zoom meeting, 6. Stay Organized: Without the physical and structural supports of traditional school, more of the organization work will fall to students (or their parents or tutors). Remember that for teenagers, being organized is very difficult. They are not just being lazy. Their brains don’t have the organizational cognitive pathways hard wired yet. This doesn’t mean that you have to do all their organizing for them, but they will most likely need help figuring out how to set up an organizational system and sticking to it. If you know an organizational whiz, whether a friend, relative or paid professional, it’s time to bring them in to help your students set up a system that will work for them. 7. Understand strengths and weaknesses: Chances are, you’ve been aware of your children’s academic strengths and weaknesses for a while, and you have already made adjustments. But now it’s time to take an assessment of their life skills – how they do in a more isolated social environment; how they organize their lives; how they manage their priorities. You may 4. Go for the grade, not the pass: It was understandable for parents to lower their standards when distance learning was sprung upon them in the spring. Classes were truncated, no one knew what to expect, and we were all just focused on survival. Things are going to be different this year. Classes and grades will be similar to traditional schools. Even if schools switch to pass/ fail, teachers will know who is putting in the effort. This will reflect directly in letters of recommendation, which will play a larger role than ever before in college applications. In addition, distance learning isn’t going to last forever, and when students go back to school, their graded classes will build on the information taught online. If students don’t learn the online material, they will have a harder time succeeding when they return to school.

Make a Classroom It doesn’t matter if it’s the kitchen table, the living room or your kid’s bedroom, but a student needs a quiet, distraction-free place that they associate with learning. Figure out where your student’s “school room” is going to be ahead of time and start making arrangements now for their “classroom” space. 3. Don’t skip class Few parents accept cutting class in physical schools, so why do parents accept it in online education? It just doesn’t seem as serious to miss a Zoom meeting, 6. Stay Organized: Without the physical and structural supports of traditional school, more of the organization work will fall to students (or their parents or tutors). Remember that for teenagers, being organized is very difficult. They are not just being lazy. Their brains don’t have the organizational cognitive pathways hard wired yet. This doesn’t mean that you have to do all their organizing for them, but they will most likely need help figuring out how to set up an organizational system and sticking to it. If you know an organizational whiz, whether a friend, relative or paid professional, it’s time to bring them in to help your students set up a system that will work for them. 7. Understand strengths and weaknesses: Chances are, you’ve been aware of your children’s academic strengths and weaknesses for a while, and you have already made adjustments. But now it’s time to take an assessment of their life skills – how they do in a more isolated social environment; how they organize their lives; how they manage their priorities. You may 4. Go for the grade, not the pass: It was understandable for parents to lower their standards when distance learning was sprung upon them in the spring. Classes were truncated, no one knew what to expect, and we were all just focused on survival. Things are going to be different this year. Classes and grades will be similar to traditional schools. Even if schools switch to pass/ fail, teachers will know who is putting in the effort. This will reflect directly in letters of recommendation, which will play a larger role than ever before in college applications. In addition, distance learning isn’t going to last forever, and when students go back to school, their graded classes will build on the information taught online. If students don’t learn the online material, they will have a harder time succeeding when they return to school. have to do some assessing of yourself, too, as you make decisions as to how to best support your children. Write lists together with your children and address those areas that you identify as weaknesses, and help each other with your strengths. Who knows, you might find through this process that your child has something to teach you during the pandemic. 8. Use District offered supplies For many families, food, computers and wi-fi can be challenging to come by. If these or any other educational necessities present a financial bind, be sure to check with your school district to find out what is available and who qualifies. And finally, go easy on yourself. It is important to remember that no generation in history has ever been asked to do what parents are doing right now. You are being asked to be a teacher, parent, breadwinner and social worker. While there certainly have been pandemics in the past, the internet has meant that parents are asked to do all of the jobs that used to be spread out across the village. Do your best, but remember that you are one person doing the work of four, and no one is perfect. Don’t beat yourself up, and get as much help as you can. Just the other day I spoke with the mother of two boys who has been feeling the loss of normality acutely. She sees her sons spending too much time alone, too much time online, too much time sitting, sleeping, eating. It’s all too much of some things and not enough of some others, and she doesn’t know what to do. A few weeks ago, in her quest to bring her sons’ lives back into balance, she had a great idea. She would take the boys on a trip. They would leave the city and have some fun in the country. She was thrilled at her plan and excited about the possibilities, and she gave herself a hearty pat on the back for orchestrating what was sure to be a transformative experience. And it was transformative – but not for her sons. The trip unfolded as planned. The family went to the country, got plenty of fresh air, played and relaxed, and afterwards – the cherry on top – her sons thanked her for all of her efforts. And yet . . . they returned A hug and a juice box. home and instantly slipped back to their pre-trip routines. She was devastated. For many parents, the pandemic is the first time they haven’t been able to fix, or even make a dent in a child’s problem. Kids suffer all kinds of hardships growing up, but attuned and creative parents are quick to find remedies ranging from a hug and a juice box to tutors, therapists, and now, learning pods. articles.text: Music Director Michael Morgan introduces Florence Price’s Symphony No. 2 Oakland Symphony is offering a weekly, archival concert series featuring past performances, with performances every Friday at 6 p.m. The current concert, Florence Price’s Symphony No. 3 in C minor, was originally premiered by the symphony on January 25, 2019 at the Paramount Theatre. Price was an African-American composer who lived from 1887 to 1953. Her First Symphony was the first work by an African-American woman to be played by a major American orchestra, the Chicago Symphony, in 1933. “She is now seeing a great rediscovery, and for me her Third Symphony is her masterpiece,” said Oakland Symphony Music Director Michael Morgan. “It is in four movements – classical in form, but American in outlook – with the melodiousness of American folk music, and the extended harmonies we have come to associate with jazz.” You can watch this performance and others in the rePAST series at https://www.oaklandsymphony.org/repast/. Price was an African-American composer who lived from 1887 to 1953. Her First Symphony was the first work by an African-American woman to be played by a major American orchestra, the Chicago Symphony, in 1933. “She is now seeing a great rediscovery, and for me her Third Symphony is her masterpiece,” said Oakland Symphony Music Director Michael Morgan. “It is in four movements – classical in form, but American in outlook – with the melodiousness of American folk music, and the extended harmonies we have come to associate with jazz.” You can watch this performance and others in the rePAST series at https://www.oaklandsymphony.org/repast/. articles.text: Did you know that Franklin Delano Roosevelt wanted to be a concert pianist? He went to the Metropolitan Opera House with his mother on November 29, 1887 to hear the young prodigy, pianist Josef Hofmann. After the concert little Franklin asked his mother: “do you think I can be a great pianist, also?” As you know, FDR did not become a great pianist. But he did rather well in another endeavor. We now will play the game of “what if”. The only difference is that everything here is the absolute truth. All the names will be familiar, but the stories behind them are not. Famed comedian Jack Benny took his music seriously. He wanted to be a great violinist more than anything else in the world. He said, somewhat ruefully, that he would gladly trade his success as a comedian if he could be a great violinist. While he rubbed shoulders with many of the greatest violinists, he never got any better; despite his disciplined practice regimen. In an effort to sound better, he purchased an outstanding Stradivarius violin and two very expensive bows. Professor Albert Einstein, on the other hand, never had any delusions about his musical ability. He loved the violin but played only for his own relaxation. Some have taken the route of glamour. The glitziest of entertainers was certainly Liberace. He realized early on that he could never compete with great concert pianists of his time, so he developed a flamboyant style and rode it to incredible success. Don’t for a minute let Liberace‘s showbiz persona fool you. He really was a fine pianist. Another person who went down the Glamour Trail was the noted cellist-composer Nina Kotova. Her reasons were completely different from Liberace‘s. Nina always wanted to be a serious concert artist, and she became an important fashion model for the sole reason of financing her concert career. The last czar of Russia, the ill-fated Nicholas II, was another violin-playing enthusiast. As was fitting a Czar, Nicolas noodled on a Stradivarius. Perhaps he should have continued down that path and avoided any military delusions. The Czar’s Stradivarius was sold by the subsequent communist government in an effort to raise money. Famed radio violinist and personality Dave Rubinoff bought the violin and used it as a successful publicity ploy. Rubinoff was another one whose musical ability far exceeded his pop musician notoriety. Such was his fame that he was the most known violinist in America. A young Jascha Heifetz wanted to go in the front door of Carnegie Hall. The doorman told him to use the musician’s entrance. Heifetz said to the doorman: “I am Jascha Heifetz”. The doorman said: “I don’t care if you’re Rubinoff. Use the musician’s entrance.” Just to be clear, Heifetz and Rubinoff were very good friends. Charlie Chaplin was not only a famous Hollywood actor, he was a composer of note and wrote some of the memorable musical themes in his movies. He, too, was an enthusiastic violinist… And a left-handed one at that. Operatic tenor Enrico Caruso was told continuously that he had no future as a singer. Somehow he managed not to be discouraged. Many of us regard Caruso as the greatest singer of all time. If he hadn’t achieved fame on the operatic stage, he would most assuredly have become a successful commercial artist. He was a featured caricaturist in newspapers and even considered syndication. And now we return to the pianist who dashed the musical career of Franklin Delano Roosevelt. Josef Hofmann is considered one of the greatest, if not THE greatest pianist of all time. He could easily have given up his musical career for that of an inventor. He had at least 70 patents to his name. He invented an improved action for the Steinway piano. Another success was his pneumatic shock absorber which was used on Pullman train cars and also for airplanes. One of his strange inventions was a house with a movable foundation so that every room of your house would always be in the sun. As a pianist, Hofmann made lots of money. But he made more money from just one of his inventions than he ever made as a famous pianist. So… as you see… the path to fame and success is often delusionary and circuitous. Pianist Joseph Hoffman made more money as an inventor than a concert pianist.

articles.text: San Francisco Ballet recently premiered a new film by Benjamin Millepied, titled Dance of Dreams. The film features SF Ballet dancers performing choreography by Justin Peck, Dwight Rhoden, Janie Taylor, and Christopher Wheeldon, all of whom donated their time to the project. It premiered on August 13 at 12 p.m., and is now available to the public on the ballet company’s live-stream “SF Ballet @ Home,” YouTube, Facebook, and IGTV. Commissioned by Helgi Tomasson and filmed in iconic San Francisco locations including the Palace of Fine Arts and the Golden Gate National Recreation Area, the six-minute film is set to “Scène d’Amour” by Bernard Hermann from the Alfred Hitchcock film Vertigo. SF Ballet Orchestra Music Director Martin West mixed and mastered the recording, which incorporates more than 150 tracks recorded remotely by more than 60 musicians in the Orchestra. Social distancing rules were observed during the filming process. The pas de deux are danced by dancers who have been sheltered in place together. You can watch the movie, and learn more about its production at https://www.sfballet.org/ sf-ballet-home/.

articles.text: Brad Pitt and Jonah Hill in a scene from Moneyball. Review by Jonathan B. Moy Our beloved, local, perennial hard-luck Oakland A’s and General Manager Billy Beane are the focus of Director Bennett Miller’s new film Moneyball, which had its world premiere on Monday night at the Paramount Theatre in downtown Oakland. It was the first major Hollywood release premiered in Oakland in 20 years. At the end of an incredible yet disappointing 2001 season in which the A’s are eliminated from post-season playoffs by the New York Yankees, Beane (with much hoopla, played by Brad Pitt) is faced with the problem of losing three key players to bigger teams with bigger money: outfielder Johnny Damon, first baseman Jason Giambi and pitcher Jason Isringhausen. Ownership will not give him the funds to replace them, so he is faced with the challenge of building a winning team with one of the smallest payrolls in Major League baseball. but it does include an improbable 20-game winning streak, the likes of which had never been seen in professional sports. The story of Moneyball is the emergence of a revolutionary, sabermetric style of baseball player evaluation, originated by statistician Bill James, and made known throughout the world from its use by Beane and Assistant GM Paul DePodesta during the early 2000’s. Flying in the face of traditional scouting methods, “moneyball” was a way to see value in traditionally undervalued players, and hence build a successful and competitive team with very limited funds. The model Beane and DePodesta created in 2002 is now utilized in some way by nearly all other major league teams, including the 2004 World Champion Boston Red Sox. Author Michael Lewis’ Moneyball must’ve been a difficult adaptation for screenwriters Steven Zaillian (a San Francisco State film school graduate who has Schindler’s List and Searching for Bobby Fischer to his credit), and Aaron Sorkin (A Few Good Men, The Social Network, “The West Wing”). Essentially it is a book about evaluating baseball players with a laptop as opposed to a scouting manual. Thankfully they were able to evoke a humanity and a meshed narrative involving the life of Beane himself. An extremely promising outfielder drafted out of high school, Beane could not rediscover his talent in the big leagues. Zaillian and Sorkin relate his lifelong frustration to the theory of “moneyball.” which values the talents of those who have been wrongly prejudged by traditional evaluation. Moneyball is actually an attempt at inclusion in a culture where exclusion is the norm. Key to the film’s success is the relationship between Beane and Brand, and the onscreen chemEnter Peter Brand (acted by Jonah Hill), youthful advisor to the Cleveland Indians, who has a new way of evaluating players that traditional scouts balk at. Facing tremendous opposition and criticism from the baseball world, including A’s manager Art Howe (played by Philip Seymour Hoffman), Beane and Brand stick to their plan of hiring those who have been written off by other teams, but who have the right numbers, including a high on-base percentage. The 2002 season does not bring a World Series Championship to Oakland,

articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré The films of Hayao Miyazaki, master storyteller and animator and often referred to as the Walt Disney of Japan, have been difficult to find in America. Through a collaboration between Studio Ghibli and HBO Max, an impressive list of Miyazaki films are now available. This week’s recommendation is Kiki’s Delivery Service, made in 1989. The film was adapted from a popular Japanese novel written by Eiko Kadono. It’s an extraordinary example of Studio Ghibli’s anime and storytelling talents, incorporating fantasy and benign crisis into a remarkable tale about a spunky young god-hearted witch on the cusp of womanhood. Kiki, now 13, as tradition dictates, must leave home. She takes her cat JiJi, a red radio, and hopes to practice her still rocky broom-flying skills. She ends up lodging with a baker for whom she begins an airborne delivery service for his freshly baked products. Beautifully crafted, saturated with rich colors, the story touches on coming-of-age issues such as independence, femininity, insecurity, friendship and even (unexpectedly for a children’s movie) sexuality, all in a warm, lighthearted manner. In essence, Kiki’s Delivery Service is also a wonderful adventure. Equally important, it is also a personal crossroads for Kiki, who, after an illness, loses her powers and must find a new purpose for her young life. It is consistently funny, optimistic, and exciting, finding and holding that coveted sweet spot that makes Miyazaki’s films simply exceptional. Kiki’s Delivery Service (1989). Written and directed by Hayao Miyazaki. With the Englishdubbed voices of Kirsten Dunst, Debbie Reynolds and Matthew Lawrence. 1 hr., 43 min. Rated G. Scene from Kiki’s Delivery Service.
articles.title: Kiki’s Delivery Service a masterpiece by Miyazaki

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré Who are these pulp fiction superheroes and why do they resonate with our children? Whatever the answer, Hollywood is in love with the comic book genre, especially with tales from the archives of DC and Marvel. This summer’s big tent blockbusters are once again defined by the superhero: Thor; X-Men: First Class; Green Lantern. And not to forget Transformers. Plus Harry Potter, a superhero to be sure. Just ask Voldermort. Now comes Marvel’s Captain America: The First Avenger. Consider the setup: a 90-pound weakling, Steve Rogers (Chris Evans), is desperate to join the army and fight the Nazis (“I hate bullies” he says), But he can’t pass the physical. He is recruited and transformed (using Super-Soldier serum) into a totally ripped G.I. Joe, aka Captain America, replete with shield, mask and tights. What 90-pound kid wouldn’t love to suddenly have the washboard abs of Captain America, an all-American hero who goes off Chris Evans stars as Captain America. to fight not just the Nazis, but a cranked up version of evil doers, an outfit called Hydra, led by Red Skull (Hugo Weaving), who also possess some serious weaponry. The first Captain America is an original film (beginning in 1942), and act one is devoted to how Rogers morphs into his present incarnation. It’s all nicely done, albeit with holes in the logic, requiring serious suspension of disbelief as well as a huge assist by CGI. But then, that’s what defines these wonderfully imagined movies. “No way” some literalists might say. Response: a chorus of kids saying, “Yes, way!” Captain America fights for truth, justice, and VE-day, which means serious combat with the Hydra. Captain America. Directed by Joe Johnston. Starring Chris Evans, Haley Atwell, Tommy Lee Jones, Hugo Weaving and Stanley Tucci. Rated PG-13. Originally printed in the Post on July 27, 2011.
articles.title: It’s summer – time for Captain America

articles.text: Steve Schiller with his electric Chevrolet Bolt. As a clean energy expert working on climate change for 25 years, Steve Schiller knows he has to “walk the walk.” Even he didn’t think he could get by with only one car that was all electric. When the lease was up on the family SUV, he and his wife Kristine decided they would try getting by with just their Chevy Bolt for a month rather than looking for another car — one of their least favorite activities. That month-long experiment has now extended into a second year. “We’re getting by fine with one car,” said Schiller, an empty nester who acknowledges his situation may be fairly unique. “My fun fact is that the best way to reduce your energy consumption is to have your kid move away,” he joked. Steve and Kristine chose the Bolt because it’s a great commuter car and perfect for any outing in the greater Bay Area. The Bolt also has a long enough range — about 250 miles on one charge — for an occasional work trip to Sacramento. Plus, access to HOV lanes on the freeway can be a real treat during commute hours. “It’s actually really fun to drive. It’s quite quick and peppy. It handles well and is comfortable. And there’s essentially no maintenance,’ he said. “You get to reduce your environmental footprint and have some fun, carefree driving.” Schiller charges the Bolt with clean energy from solar panels he installed on his roof nearly 10 years ago. He estimates he spends only $200 a year on electricity from the grid, and that’s largely because of charging the car (and a hot tub). He admits his Bolt isn’t as sleek as a Tesla but doesn’t see that as a disadvantage. “I take night classes at Laney in ceramics and don’t have to worry about parking a fancy car,” he says. “It’s a very practical car.” Seeing more electric cars in Piedmont Schiller served on the Piedmont Climate Action Plan Task Force and is an expert on clean energy policy and implementation. Electrifying the transportation sector is key to addressing climate change, he stated, noting that about 40% of greenhouse gas emissions in California and about 42% of Piedmont’s emissions are associated with transportation, mostly passenger cars. “Passenger vehicles are a big deal,” he says. “Eventually we have to get rid of gasoline as the primary transportation fuel source for personal vehicles and trucks.” He acknowledged that in addition to people buying electric vehicles, there is a need for more infrastructure – namely charging stations – to support widespread adoption of electric vehicles. And that’s why he supports a proposed pilot project to install seven EV fast-charging stations in three different locations in Piedmont at no cost to the city. “The bottom line is you have to build the infrastructure,” he said. He believes the fast-charging stations may be most valuable for people like teachers and city staff who drive to Piedmont regularly for work. “You need to try projects and experiment to see what technologies and strategies will be adopted as cost-effective and convenient common practices,” he explained. “Piedmont is a good community for innovation.” To watch a video of interviews with Steve Schiller and other electric vehicle owners in Piedmont, visit https://youtu.be/ OE3a9yTBeTA. Climate Corner is a collaboration between the city of Piedmont and Piedmont Connect, a local environmental nonprofit, to raise awareness about climate actions in our community. articles.text: This week Chabot Space & Science Center is celebrating its 20th anniversary on Skyline Boulevard in Oakland, and 137 years in Oakland. An online silent auction to benefit STEM education at the Center Chabot’s special silent auction will continue until September 1. Items to bid on include private telescope viewings, prints from the Luminous Moon exhibition, a party with a scientist and an exclusive Hike and Sip event. Throughout August Chabot Space & Science Center encourages the community to share their favorite memories from the past 20 years on Facebook, Instagram and Twitter with #ChabotSpaceMemories. Chabot Observatory opened in 1883 at Lafayette Square in Oakland as the official timekeeper of the city. In 1918, Chabot moved outside the city center to Mountain Boulevard for clearer skies and astronomical visibility. It expanded with a 90-seat planetarium, science labs and classrooms. In collaboration with NASA, Chabot Space & Science Center moved to its current location on Skyline Boulevard in August 2000. Since then, the Center has grown with interactive unique exhibits, otherworldly NASA artifacts and cutting edge technology to drive scientific curiosity. For details on the events call 510-336-7300. articles.text: Ray Simpson Stewart, a pioneer in the development of the Silicon Valley electronics industry, passed away on Saturday, August 1st at his home in Redwood City due to complications from non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma. He was 93. Ray first came to the Palo Alto area in 1953 when he was asked by his employer, Convair, to participate in the testing of Vertical Takeoff and Landing (VTOL) aircraft at Moffett Field in Mountain View. From there, he became involved with the development of the video recorder at Ampex Corporation. He and several colleagues from Ampex formed Datamec Corp., which was sold to Hewlett Packard in 1965. He then became President of Data Memory, Inc., a company that produced instant replay for television. Ray continued to engage in entrepreneurial endeavors in the electronics industry in Silicon Valley for the remainder of his career. Born in Honolulu, Hawaii on December 16, 1926, Ray was the second son of Col. William Robert Stewart and Mary Agnes Simpson. His father was a career Army officer, which led the family to live in numerous places around the world, including Alcatraz Island, where Col. Stewart was the last military warden of the prison prior to it becoming a Federal penitentiary in 1934. The family then moved to Corregidor, Philippines, and Fort Stevens, Oregon, where Col. Stewart was the commanding officer. He next lived in Seattle prior to finally settling in La Jolla, just before World War II. ing the USATF Masters Outdoor Championships in Eugene, Oregon in 1994. He was part of a team that continues to hold the world record for the Men’s age 70+ in the 4x800 relay set at the USATF Masters Outdoor Championships in San Jose in 1997. He became an active member and Executive Director of Fifty Plus, an organization to promote fitness for seniors. Ray was also an avid adventurer and enjoyed traveling with his family to all parts of the world. Ray Stewart is survived by his younger brother, Stanley Hays Stewart (Masako), of La Jolla, and five children: Sandra MacPhail (Jack) of Portland; Claire Kostic (Mark) formerly of Piedmont, and currently Atherton; Sharon Stewart of Ukiah; Kim Stewart of Los Altos; and David Stewart (Paula) of Los Altos. In addition, he is survived by nine grandchildren: Sheldon Stevenson, Jeffrey Stevenson, Creighton Stevenson, Kirsten Hanafee, Sean Hanafee, Emily Bortz, Edward Bortz, Camila Stewart and Giana Stewart, and two great-grandchildren, Finn Stevenson and Charles Stevenson. He is predeceased by Norma Pappas, his second wife, whom he married in 2006, and by his older brother, William Stewart, Jr. of San Antonio, Texas. Due to circumstances related to the COVID-19 pandemic, burial services and a celebration of his life will be private. The family requests that in lieu of flowers memorial donations be made to Stanford Medicine Cancer Discovery Fund, the Lymphoma Research Foundation, or Pathways Hospice.
