articles.text: Due to the impact of COVID-19, the Oakland Museum Women’s Board has made the decision to postpone for one year its annual White Elephant Sale in 2021. Both the Preview Sale scheduled for January 2021 and the two-day Sale in March 2021 will be rescheduled in 2022. The decision was made to ensure the safety of the volunteers, shoppers, and donors who participate in the much-anticipated sale each year. Up to 1,000 dedicated volunteers organize the 96,000 square foot warehouse year-round in preparation for the sale. Unfortunately, this cannot safely be done this year due to COVID-19. For the past five years the White Elephant Sale has generated over $2 million each year to support the Oakland Museum of California. The Women’s Board is currently evaluating alternative strategies to raise funds for the Museum. Donors currently are being asked to hold onto the items they wish to donate. For more information, visit the Oakland Museum Women’s Board website at whiteelephantsale.org. The Oakland Museum of California greatly appreciates the hard work and generosity of all the past, present, and future White Elephant Sale volunteers. The museum staff and board are sad to miss this time-honored tradition, one of the biggest and best rummage sales in California for more than 60 years.
articles.title: White Elephant Sale postponed for one year

articles.text: Once again, the bicycle team, Linda and Marvin, will be riding in memory of Linda Lettieri and Marvin Stern, both of whom passed away from ALS (Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis, better known as Lou Gehrig¹s Disease). July 9 marked the 13th anniversary of Linda¹s passing and the 15th year our bicycle team, Team Linda and Marvin, will be participating in the Ride to Defeat ALS. This is truly a science fiction-like disease in its progressive reduction of your ability to move, speak and eventually, breathe. Since ALS is currently not well understood, has no cure or effective treatment path, we are working hard to fund-raise to find a cure through the ALS Association, Golden West Chapter. Finally, there are some glimmers of hope that some of the genetics of ALS are being discovered, although we are a long way from effective treatments and the eventual cure. The ALS Association is the only non-profit organization fighting Lou Gehrig’s Disease on every front. By leading the way in global research, providing assistance for people with ALS through a nationwide network of chapters, coordinating multidisciplinary care through certified clinical care centers, and fostering government partnerships, The Association builds hope and enhances quality of life while Riders raise money for the ALS Association in last years ride. Because of the Coronavirus, this year’s ride will be virtual. aggressively searching for new treatments and a cure. Team Linda and Marvin will be riding Saturday, September 26 in their memory and we are soliciting your support to help our team exceed our fundraising goal for ALS research. Last year, through the amazingly generous donations of friends, family, and clients, we raised over $70,000 for ALS Research. The timeline for a cure or even a treatment for ALS may be very long, and we may not be around long enough to see it, but the goal is worthy of our effort and hopefully your dollars. Any contribution, no matter how small (or large!) will be appreciated and will help fund research into the causes and cures of ALS. Your tax-deductible gift will make a difference in the lives of many! It is faster and easier than ever to support this great cause. This year, due to the Coronavirus, the ride is going virtual, but some of us will be riding from Oakland to the top of Mount Diablo and back, a distance of 80 miles and 7,500 feet of vertical climbing. Born in Honolulu, Hawaii on December 16, 1926, Ray was the second son of Col. William Robert Stewart and Mary Agnes Simpson. Stewart was the last military warden of the prison prior to it becoming a Federal penitentiary in 1934. The family then moved to Corregidor, Philippines, and Fort Stevens, Oregon, where Col. Stewart was the commanding officer. He next lived in Seattle prior to finally settling in La Jolla, just before World War II. ing the USATF Masters Outdoor Championships in Eugene, Oregon in 1994. He was part of a team that continues to hold the world record for the Men’s age 70+ in the 4x800 relay set at the USATF Masters Outdoor Championships in San Jose in 1997. Ray was also an avid adventurer and enjoyed traveling with his family to all parts of the world. articles.text: The status-quo is a comforting concept for most of us. Especially as we age and our bodies change, it is more convenient to get used to “the new normal” rather than asking for help or taking action. The pandemic has shattered this complacency and highlighted our abilities and/or disabilities. Home care normally begins when someone experiences a long-term care event. This can be anything from a trip or fall, to the diagnosis of a chronic illness like Alzheimer’s or Parkinson’s Disease. On the other hand, the normal aging process takes its toll on all of us. Some people reach out for help early on, which can relieve some daily stress and improve health outcomes, but most people wait until they are facing a precipitous decline. The Coronavirus has disrupted the daily lives of nearly everyone on the planet. Although it is not a typical long-term care event, people are being forced to change the way they do things. The experience is illustrating just how interdependent we all are. Those at risk of acute COVID-19- related complications are told to avoid leaving their homes unless absolutely necessary. But how is this possible without relying on others? These individuals need help from a caregiver who can assist with essential errands and provide much-needed connection. In a previous article, Physical Distancing vs. Social Distancing, I shared that “feelings of isolation and loneliness have been found to have physical consequences such as increased risk of depression, heart disease, and even dementia”. Before COVID, isolation was an epidemic among seniors and the disabled. Now it is compounded by the fear of contracting the droplet-borne disease. It is important to count your blessings when things seem bleak. For the younger and healthier individuals among us, a Coronavirus infection may be rather mild. Those with family or friends nearby during the pandemic will not go without companionship. But far too many will suffer in silence and not get the help they need. If you can be counted among the latter, or know someone in this situation, reach out for assistance. Break out of the status-quo and speak up. Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. Dear MacMama: I know that backing up your computer is a good idea, and I have a little hard drive attached to my iMac which I use for my Time Machine backup. But I have been hearing about “cloud” backups, and with earthquakes and wildfire season, I worry that the attached drive is not enough to safeguard all of my stuff. Can you explain how it works and what is “the cloud”? Sima, Piedmont Dear Sima: You are absolutely right. A physical backup, one that is on an external drive, is not enough if you want to make sure your data is protected. It’s important to configure and keep a “cloud” backup as well as a physical one as an added security for your precious data. What that means is that you use your internet connection and the proprietary software of whichever company you pay to back up your data. Just as Time Machine backs up your computer to an external drive every hour, you will set a schedule for your data to back up to the cloud. What is the cloud? According to PCMAG, “…In the simplest terms, cloud computing means storing and accessing data and programs over the internet instead of your computer’s hard drive. ... Ultimately, the “cloud” is just a metaphor for the internet.” But as far as storing files, companies have servers (physical storage drives) that can receive data through the internet. So, for example, the company that I use for backup, Code42, who has a product called “Crash Plan”, has actual physical servers that contain storage drives, and I use the “cloud”, or the internet, to back up my files to their servers. If I want to restore copies of my files, I have to use the internet to download them back to my computer. It is not necessary or wise to back up applications, as they can be replaced, only documents, spreadsheets, presentations, music, movies, pictures, etc. Google Drive and Gmail is another cloud computing interface. If you access your Gmail through the web, like Safari or Chrome, you are accessing those emails and files through the cloud. They don’t live on your computer, but you can access, edit, and share them with others without ever actually downloading them to your own computer. If you have a business version of Google Work, you get 30 GB of storage for each user and can work on hundreds of documents without ever downloading them. And if your computer crashes, or is incapacitated, your files on Google drive and Gmail are safe, and all you have to do on a replacement (or any) computer, is to sign into your Gmail account. In reality, you may already have a cloud backup and not be aware of it. If you chose to use iCloud Desktop and Documents, or iCloud Photos when you set up your Mac, or initiated it later, you already have a “cloud” backp of those items. And if you get a new computer, you can sign into iCloud and download all of your data to your new Mac. If you store any files in Dropbox, those items are also backed up in Dropbox’s servers. You can access them from any computer, or your phone or iPad with an internet connection. articles.text: I recently came across an article in a professional trade magazine which discussed fighting coronavirus with food. It stated that proper nutrition can help individuals fight the coronavirus. Eating healthy helps you fight all diseases more effectively – not just COVID-19. It improves your mood and energy level and reduces anxiety and depression. Every little bit of healthy eating helps your body fight disease more effectively. According to the World Health Organization, eating a healthy diet is very important during the COVID-19 pandemic. What we eat and drink can affect our body’s ability to prevent, fight and recover from infections. While no foods or dietary supplements can prevent or cure COVID-19 infection, healthy diets are important for supporting immune systems. Good nutrition can also reduce the likelihood of developing other health problems, including obesity, heart disease, diabetes and some types of cancer. This article got me thinking how fortunate we are here at the Lake Merritt-Independent Senior Community. First of all, we have an amazing executive chef, Michael Cook. For 18 years, Cook was the executive chef at the very popular À Côté, a trendy restaurant in Oakland’s Rockridge district. For his part, Cook has embraced his role at The Lake Merritt. His philosophy is to incorporate, whenever possible, local and regionally grown foods. He is extremely conscientious about the nutritional needs of our population. “I love cooking for the residents, and they must love it too because they keep coming back for more,” Cook said Not only do we have delicious food, we also have in our possession one of Oakland’s best kept secrets – the Terrace Room. Known to many as a little gem, it is tucked inside our community with its panoramic views of Lake Merritt. In the 1930s and 1940s the Terrace Room was the city’s hot spot, featuring great cocktails and dining along with dancing and Big Bands, including the famed Count Basie. I mention the Terrace Room because it has been beneficial in helping us fight off social isolation. During this pandemic we have been following CDC recommendations, including wearing masks and social distancing. However, it is important to remember that mental health also cannot be overlooked. The Terrace Room is over 4,000 square feet, with high ceilings, great ventilation and windows that open directly onto the lake. It can seat 300 people, and because of the large space we are able to spread the dining tables out eight feet apart. Thus, we have created seating for all our residents who can dine at a distance from each other and yet they are still able to socialize. This beautiful restaurant allows us to meet the nutritional needs of our residents as well as allowing us to maintain socialization and social distancing that helps them stay emotionally, mentally and physically strong. We look forward to the day when we can once again invite guests to join us in this lovely and historic restaurant. Until that time, everyone is grateful to have the opportunity to live here at The Lake Merritt where the food is delicious, and residents don’t have to worry about feeling isolated. Tim Johnson is Executive Director of The Lake Merritt-Independent Senior Living, 1800 Madison Street, Oakland. 510-903-3600 www.thelakemerritt.com.

articles.text: New ordinance requiring rigorous vegetation upkeep in effect next month The southeastern portion of Piedmont is now declared a Very High Fire Severity Zone by Cal Fire, and residents will have to be vigilant with managing their landscaping when a new ordinance goes into effect on Wednesday, September 16. A second reading of the ordinance was unanimously approved by the city council at its meeting this week on August 17. The newly created Very High Fire Severity Zone includes most of the area between La Salle Avenue to Park Boulevard, although a few neighborhoods are exempt. It also includes the area surrounding Tyson Lake. The zone is part of a wider designation that runs through the Oakland Hills. All of Piedmont was recently declared a Wildland Urban Interface Fire Area by the state. Residents living in the Very High Fire Severity Zone will have to cut down and remove hazardous vegetation, like dead trees or brush, from the property. There must be a 30-foot perimeter around each structure that is a “defensible space,” meaning an area where wildfire prevention practices are in place. Roadways must be kept clear of vegetation. Additionally, roofs and gutters need to be regularly cleaned and maintained. The Piedmont Fire Department indicated several plants and trees that are considered flammaFire Hazard Severity Zones VHFHSZ Non-VHFHSZ Image courtesy of Cal Fire A map indicating the Very High Fire Hazard Severity Zone in Piedmont. ble vegetation, including California Bay Laurel, Cedar, Cypress, Eucalyptus, Fir, Palm, Pine, Manzanita and Pampas grass. “These proposed changes provide minimum vegetation management standards, in an effort to decrease the likelihood of ignition of a structure during direct flame impingement or exposure to burning embers projected by a wildfire,” Fire Chief Bret Black explained in a report. The designation of the zone has been in the works for over a year. It was initially spurred on Piedmont’s adoption of a Hazard Mitigation Plan adopted in 2019. “Every part of what were proposing really just ticks off the mitigations” put forth by the plan, Black told Council this week, adding that the PFD also looked at wildfire mitigation plans from Oakland and elsewhere in the region. Black noted that residents seemed interested in reducing the possibility of widespread wildfire damage in Piedmont. “Engagement is very much reciprocal,” he noted. Mayor Bob McBain noted that usually people have negative reactions about discussions of code changes, but this ordinance is critical because it is a matter of public safety. “I think we need to recall and remind ourselves that Bret and our fine fire department are here to protect us, more than anything else, and keep us safe,” McBain said. “I think this code reflects it.” Taking a few simple steps now can make a big difference in reducing the risk of wildfire and increasing the safety for you and your family. Piedmont Firefighters have already begun preparing for the upcoming fire season, and we are asking Piedmont residents to do the same. A great place to start is online at: • Identify vegetation hazards and make a plan to deal with them • Make a simple plan in case of evacuation. • Pay attention to information and instructions in the event of an emergency. Look for additional information and tips that will make the community as safe as it can be this upcoming summer. If you have any questions or need assistance, feel free to contact the Piedmont Fire Department at 510-420-3030.

At Piedmont Middle School, the first day of school in 2020 was missing the traditional sixth grade donut hole and orange juice breakfast before class. But with new challenges come new solutions, and Piedmont parents will lead the way in finding creative ways to make school meaningful.
